concepts.name: What is a constitution and why we need one
concepts.description: The meaning of a constitution, what it contains, and why a rulebook matters, with the Indian Constitution as an example.
concepts.idea: A constitution is a rulebook for a nation that sets out its basic principles, government, rights and duties.
concepts.rule: A constitution is a document that spells out a nation's basic principles and laws. It lays out the framework and roles of the three organs of government, checks and balances among them, the rights and duties of citizens and the long-term goals of the nation. The kabaddi example shows that a rulebook settles disputes. The Indian Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, is preserved in a helium-filled glass case, has 25 parts and 12 schedules (22 parts and 8 schedules at the start) and is the world's largest written constitution. Officials pledge to uphold it.
concepts.example: The kabaddi referee used the rulebook to settle a dispute.

questions.q: Constitutions are classified into evolved and enacted types. Which one of the following is a feature of an enacted constitution?
questions.a: It is deliberately made by a constituent assembly, or promulgated by a king or a parliament, and set out in a document
o: It is deliberately made by a constituent assembly, or promulgated by a king or a parliament, and set out in a document
It is the outcome of a slow and gradual process and rests mainly on conventions, practices, principles and judicial decisions
It can be amended in the same manner as ordinary laws and does not need any special procedure of amendment at all
It assumes a broad consensus on common societal goals which the public authorities are required to strive to achieve
questions.e: An enacted constitution is deliberately made by a constituent assembly or constitutional council, or promulgated by a king or parliament, and is in the form of a book or documents; the American and Indian Constitutions are the examples. The evolved type (British) rests on conventions and judicial decisions; flexibility and the prescriptive archetype are different classifications.
w: Describes an evolved (cumulative) constitution such as the British one, not an enacted one.
Describes a flexible constitution; flexibility is a separate classification based on the method of amendment.
Describes a prescriptive constitution in Bulmer's procedural-prescriptive classification.

questions.q: Which one of the following countries is an example of a state having an unwritten constitution?
questions.e: The constitutions of the USA, Japan, France, Germany and India are examples of written constitutions, while those of the UK, New Zealand and Israel are examples of unwritten ones, found in conventions, practices, charters, statutes and judicial decisions.
w: Germany has a written (codified) constitution, its Basic Law, and so is not an example of an unwritten one.
Japan is a written-constitution state, like the USA, France and India.
France is one of the written (codified) constitutions; the unwritten examples are the UK, New Zealand and Israel.

questions.q: In a country with a written constitution, a ruler uses a clause of that very document to wield unlimited power, and no institution can check him. Which one of the following conclusions is in line with the theory of constitutionalism?
questions.a: A constitution exists but constitutionalism does not, since arbitrary power conferred even by a document negates it
o: A constitution exists but constitutionalism does not, since arbitrary power conferred even by a document negates it
The country enjoys constitutionalism, because the ruler's power flows from a written and codified constitutional document
The country enjoys constitutionalism, because a constitution that vests power in one person is a limited government by definition
The country has neither a constitution nor constitutionalism, because a document permitting such power cannot be called a constitution
questions.e: A country may have a constitution but not constitutionalism, as in a dictatorship; constitutionalism means limited government, and arbitrary power in the hands of any individual or institution, even if conferred by a constitutional document, is a negation of it.
w: Contradicts the theory: arbitrary power conferred by a constitutional document is a negation of constitutionalism.
A government with unlimited power is the opposite of limited government, which is the core of constitutionalism.
A country may have a constitution but not constitutionalism, as in a dictatorship; so it does have a constitution.

questions.q: The Constitution as adopted in 1949 contained which one of the following?
questions.a: A Preamble, 395 Articles divided into 22 Parts, and 8 Schedules
o: A Preamble, 395 Articles divided into 22 Parts, and 8 Schedules
A Preamble, 395 Articles divided into 25 Parts, and 8 Schedules
A Preamble, about 470 Articles divided into 22 Parts, and 12 Schedules
A Preamble, 395 Articles divided into 22 Parts, and 12 Schedules
questions.e: Originally (1949) a Preamble, 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; presently about 470 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules. The Class 7 chapter text gives the same Parts and Schedules (22 and 8 at the start, 25 and 12 now).
w: The 25 Parts is the present count, not the 1949 count.
About 470 Articles and 12 Schedules are the present figures.
12 Schedules is the present count; the original Constitution had 8.

questions.q: Critics have called the Indian Constitution 'elephantine' because it is too bulky and too detailed. In terms of the qualities of a good constitution, this criticism points to the absence of
questions.e: Brevity means being precise and without unwanted provisions, since a lengthy document with too many details creates confusion. Critics of the Indian Constitution charge it with 'elephantine size': too bulky, too detailed, with unnecessary elements.
w: A bulky document is comprehensive; the complaint is about excess detail, not about gaps.
Adaptability means being able to change with the times; bulk does not concern it.
Stability means that the constitution is not easily tampered with; bulk does not concern it.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the classification of constitutions:

1. The Constitution of the United Kingdom is an enacted, codified document.
2. Lord James Bryce is the originator of the rigid-flexible classification.
3. The Constitutions of the UK and New Zealand are given as examples of flexible (elastic) constitutions.
4. India's Constitution is classified as a mixture of the rigid and flexible types.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the UK has an evolved constitution found in conventions, statutes, charters and judicial decisions, not in a single codified document. Statement 2 is correct: the rigid-flexible classification is Lord James Bryce's. Statement 3 is correct: the UK and New Zealand are the usual flexible (elastic) examples. Statement 4 is correct: India's Constitution is neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible but a synthesis of both.
w: '1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect (the UK constitution is not a single codified document), and leaves out statement 4, which is correct.
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 4, which is correct: India's Constitution is also a synthesis of the rigid and flexible types.
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 1, which is incorrect since the UK constitution is evolved and unwritten.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the purposes of a constitution as identified by the scholar Elliot Bulmer:

1. Declaring and defining the boundaries of the political community lies outside the purposes that Bulmer identifies.
2. Among Bulmer's purposes is binding a state to given social, economic or developmental aims.
3. Bulmer's list says that establishing and regulating political institutions is a task left to ordinary legislation, not to a constitution.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the first purpose in Bulmer's list is to declare and define the boundaries of the political community. Statement 2 is correct: committing states to social, economic or developmental goals is the eighth purpose listed. Statement 3 is incorrect: the fifth purpose is that a constitution can establish and regulate the political institutions of the community.
w: '3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: establishing political institutions is a constitutional purpose, not one left to ordinary law; and statement 2 is correct.
'1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect: declaring the boundaries of the political community is Bulmer's first purpose.
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: institutions are to be established and regulated by the constitution in Bulmer's list.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about constitutionalism:

1. Constitutionalism connotes limited government and is the antithesis of arbitrary power.
2. According to Wheare, constitutional government means government limited by the terms of a constitution, not merely by the desires and capacities of those who exercise power.
3. Among the elements of constitutionalism listed by Louis Henkin are civilian control of the military and police governed by law and judicial control.
4. Proportional representation in elections is one of the eight elements of constitutionalism listed by Louis Henkin.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: constitutionalism connotes limited government and is the antithesis of arbitrary power. Statement 2 is correct: K.C. Wheare defined constitutional government as government limited by the terms of a constitution, not merely by the desires and capacities of those who exercise power. Statement 3 is correct: Louis Henkin lists civilian control of the military and police governed by law and judicial control among his eight elements. Statement 4 is incorrect: his eight are popular sovereignty, rule of law, democratic government, separation of powers, independent judiciary, civilian control of the military, police governed by law and respect for individual rights.
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: proportional representation is not a Henkin element, and Wheare's definition (statement 2) is correct.

'2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: proportional representation is not a Henkin element, and the limited-government point (statement 1) is correct.
'1 and 2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: statement 3 on Henkin's elements (civilian control of the military, police under law) is also correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the characteristics of a good constitution:

1. Brevity: a bulky constitution that carries excessive detail makes it harder to interpret its clauses.
2. Clarity: a constitution should state its provisions in clear terms, since complicated language lowers understanding.
3. Adaptability: a constitution should be dynamic and not static, able to adapt itself to changing situations and requirements.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: brevity means precision without unwanted provisions, since excessive detail creates confusion in interpretation. Statement 2 is correct: clarity means clear terms, since complicated language lowers understanding. Statement 3 is correct: adaptability means the constitution is a living document that adapts to changing situations.
w: '1 and 2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: adaptability (statement 3) is also a quality of a good constitution.
'1 and 3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: clarity (statement 2) is also a quality of a good constitution.
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct: brevity (statement 1) is also a quality of a good constitution.

2. It is the Prime Minister alone who takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, while the President merely promises to follow its provisions.
3. The original Constitution is preserved in a helium-filled glass case because helium does not react with paper or ink.

Statement 2 is incorrect: the chapter says the President takes the oath to preserve, protect and defend it; the Union ministers and judges promise to follow its provisions. Statement 3 is correct. Statement 4 is correct: the fourth item in the chapter's list. (Class 7 Social Science chapter text (Exploring Society, Grade 7 Part 1, ch.10).)

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about federal and unitary constitutions:

1. A federal constitution divides power between the national and the regional governments and lets them operate independently in their own jurisdictions.
2. Under a unitary constitution the regional governments exercise their powers independently of the national government.
3. The UK, France, Japan and China are among the countries in which a unitary constitution is prevalent.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: a federal constitution divides power between the national and regional governments, each independent in its sphere. Statement 2 is incorrect: under a unitary constitution regional governments are subordinate agencies exercising only powers delegated by the national government. Statement 3 is correct: the UK, France, Japan, China, Italy and Norway are among the unitary states.
w: '1 and 2 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct: regional governments in a unitary system exercise only delegated powers, and statement 3 is correct.
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect: statement 2 is incorrect: unitary regional governments are subordinate to the national government.
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: statement 1 on federal division of power is also correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Parts and Articles of the Constitution:

1. Articles 324 to 329 together form Part XV, the part on elections.
2. Articles 352 to 360 together form Part XVIII, the part on emergency provisions.
3. Part III, the part on Fundamental Rights, extends from Article 12 up to Article 51.
4. Part IX-A, on the Municipalities, was added by the 74th Amendment Act of 1992.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Part XV on elections covers Articles 324 to 329. Statement 2 is correct: Part XVIII on emergency provisions covers Articles 352 to 360. Statement 3 is incorrect: Part III covers Articles 12 to 35; Articles 36 to 51 form Part IV on the Directive Principles. Statement 4 is correct: the 74th Amendment Act of 1992 inserted Part IX-A on the Municipalities.
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: Part III ends at Article 35, and Part XV (statement 1) is correct.
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: Part III ends at Article 35, and the Municipalities part (statement 4) is correct.
'1 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: Part XVIII on emergency provisions (statement 2) is also correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about important Articles of the Constitution:

1. Article 123 empowers the Governor to promulgate ordinances during the recess of the state legislature.
2. Article 161 gives the Governor the power to grant pardons and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases.
3. Article 239AA contains special provisions with respect to Delhi.
4. The council of ministers that aids and advises the Governor is provided for in Article 74.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Article 123 is the President's ordinance power; the Governor's is Article 213. Statement 2 is correct: Article 161 gives the Governor pardoning powers in cases within the state's executive power. Statement 3 is correct: Article 239AA makes special provisions for Delhi. Statement 4 is incorrect: Article 74 concerns the council of ministers that aids and advises the President; for the Governor it is Article 163.
w: '1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect (Article 213 is the Governor's ordinance power), and leaves out statement 3, which is correct: leaves out statement 3, which is correct (Article 239AA); and Article 213 is the Governor's ordinance power.
'2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect (Article 74 is the President's council of ministers): Article 74 is the President's council of ministers; the Governor's is Article 163.
'1, 3 and 4 only' includes statements 1 and 4, which are incorrect, and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: statements 1 and 4 are incorrect, and statement 2 (Article 161) is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the procedural and prescriptive archetypes of constitutions:

1. Under a procedural constitution the structures of public institutions are defined and legal limits on government power are set to protect democratic processes and rights.
2. A prescriptive constitution assumes, or attempts to impose, a broad consensus on common societal goals that public authorities must strive to achieve.
3. The difference between the two archetypes rests on the method of amending the document.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: a procedural constitution defines institutional structures and the legal limits of government power. Statement 2 is correct: a prescriptive constitution assumes a broad consensus on societal goals that authorities must pursue. Statement 3 is incorrect: the difference relates to the nature and purposes of the document itself; the method of amendment is the basis of the rigid-flexible classification.
w: '2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: the archetypes do not depend on the amendment method, and statement 1 is correct.
'1 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: the archetypes do not depend on the amendment method, and statement 2 is correct.
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: statement 3 is incorrect: amendment method distinguishes rigid from flexible constitutions.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the meaning of a constitution:

1. The word 'constitution' is derived from the Latin word constituere, meaning to establish or set up.
2. Wade and Phillips describe a constitution as a document having a special legal sanctity that sets out the framework and principal functions of the organs of government.
3. Wheare's definition confines a constitution to the rules governing the legislature and leaves out the rest of the system of government.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is correct. Statement 3 is incorrect: Wheare describes it as the whole system of government of a country, the collection of rules which establish and regulate or govern the government. So exactly 2 are correct.
w: Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not 1.
Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not 3.
Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not none.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the number of Articles in some constitutions as originally framed:

1. When first written, the American Constitution had just seven Articles.
2. The Australian Constitution originally consisted of 128 Articles.
3. The Canadian Constitution originally consisted of 138 Articles.
4. The Chinese Constitution originally consisted of 147 Articles.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: the American Constitution had seven Articles. Statement 2 is correct: the Australian Constitution had 128 Articles. Statement 3 is incorrect: Canada had 147; the figure 138 belongs to the Chinese Constitution. Statement 4 is incorrect: China had 138; the figure 147 belongs to the Canadian Constitution. So exactly 2 are correct.
w: Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not 1.
Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not 3.
Miscount: exactly 2 of the statements are correct, not 4.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements based on the Class 7 Social Science chapter:

1. Many constitutions, including the Indian one, state the values and ideals the country is committed to, such as equality and justice for all, fraternity, pluralism and freedom.
2. The values and ideals of a society are an ornamental addition, and the laws and principles in a constitution are framed independently of them.
3. A constitution describes how laws are made, but who elects the executive and how the judiciary is made are matters it leaves out.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect: the chapter says these values and ideals usually form the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution. Statement 3 is incorrect: the chapter says a constitution describes how laws are made and implemented, who elects the executive, how the judiciary is made, and what rights and duties citizens have. So exactly 1 are correct. (Class 7 Social Science chapter text (Exploring Society, Grade 7 Part 1, ch.10).)
w: Miscount: exactly 1 of the statements are correct, not 2.
Miscount: exactly 1 of the statements are correct, not 3.
Miscount: exactly 1 of the statements are correct, not none.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: Stability is listed among the qualities of a good constitution.
Statement-II: Suitability requires a constitution to suit the historical, socio-cultural, economic and political conditions of the nation.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Stability (the constitution should facilitate political stability and not allow easy tampering) and suitability (it must suit the historical, socio-cultural, economic and political conditions of the nation). Both are correct but separate qualities; neither explains the other.
w: Rejected: suitability to national conditions is a separate quality, not the reason stability is listed.
Rejected: Statement-II is correct.
Rejected: Statement-I is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: India's Constitution blends the features of a rigid and a flexible constitution.
Statement-II: Every provision of the Constitution can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament in the manner of ordinary legislation.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

questions.q:
Match the scholar in List-I with the idea associated with him in List-II.

List-I (Scholar)
A. Lord James Bryce
B. K.C. Wheare
C. Elliot Bulmer
D. Louis Henkin

List-II (Idea)
1. Classified constitutions as rigid or flexible
2. Described the Indian Constitution as quasi-federal
3. Identified eight elements of constitutionalism

concepts.name: The Constituent Assembly and the writing of the Constitution
concepts.description: Why a constitution was needed, the Constituent Assembly, its members, the Drafting Committee and important dates.
concepts.idea: The Constituent Assembly wrote the Constitution in almost three years, adopting it on 26 November 1949.
concepts.rule: While India was struggling for independence, questions arose about the type of government, rules, voting rights and settling disputes. A Constituent Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946 with 389 members, reduced to 299 after Partition, including 15 women, elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was its Chairman. The Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the first Law and Justice minister. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.
concepts.example: Members were elected by provincial legislatures, who were in turn elected by the people.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly was not elected directly by the people on adult franchise. Which one of the following describes how its members from British India were chosen under the Cabinet Mission scheme?
questions.a: Provincial legislators voted separately as Muslims, Sikhs and General, each group electing its seats by the single transferable vote
o: Provincial legislators voted separately as Muslims, Sikhs and General, each group electing its seats by the single transferable vote
They were elected by all adults in single-member territorial constituencies, by the first-past-the-post method of voting
They were nominated by the Viceroy from among the leaders of the Congress, the Muslim League and the minority communities
They were chosen by the members of the Congress Working Committee, which then allotted seats to the other parties by agreement
questions.e: Seats of each British province were divided among Muslims, Sikhs and General, and each community's representatives were elected by that community in the provincial legislative assembly through proportional representation by single transferable vote. Class 7 Social Science chapter text (Exploring Society, Grade 7 Part 1, ch.10): members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people.
w: Adult franchise was not used; the members were indirectly elected (the chapter text,says elected by the provincial legislative assemblies).
Nominations were used only for the princely states, whose representatives were nominated by their rulers.
No party body chose the members; provincial assemblies elected them community-wise.

questions.q: Which one of the following pairs of a committee of the Constituent Assembly and its chairman is correctly matched?
questions.e: The Steering Committee and the Rules of Procedure Committee were chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad; the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees by Nehru; the Provincial Constitution Committee by Sardar Patel; the Minorities Sub-Committee by H.C. Mukherjee and the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee by J.B. Kripalani.
w: Nehru, not Patel, chaired the Union Powers Committee.
Patel, not Nehru, chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee.
H.C. Mukherjee chaired the Minorities Sub-Committee; Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the time taken in making the Constitution is correct?
questions.a: The Drafting Committee sat for 141 days, while the Assembly considered the Draft Constitution for 114 days
o: The Drafting Committee sat for 141 days, while the Assembly considered the Draft Constitution for 114 days
The Drafting Committee sat for 114 days, while the Assembly considered the Draft Constitution for 141 days
The Drafting Committee sat for 141 days, while the Assembly considered the Draft Constitution for 214 days
The Drafting Committee sat for 114 days, while the Assembly considered the Draft Constitution for 414 days

w: The two figures are interchanged.
The Assembly considered the draft for 114 days, not 214.
Both figures are wrong: 141 days for the Drafting Committee and 114 for the Assembly.

questions.q: Most of the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, but a few provisions came into force earlier, on 26 November 1949 itself. Which one of the following was among them?
questions.a: Article 324, vesting superintendence of elections in the Election Commission

Article 14, guaranteeing equality before the law to all persons in the territory of India
Article 32, providing the remedy of writs for enforcing fundamental rights in the Supreme Court
Article 368, laying down the procedure of amendment and the powers of Parliament

Articles 14, 32 and 368 are named in Ch.4 but are not in the early list.

Article 32 came into force on 26 January 1950.
Article 368 came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Why was 26 January chosen as the date of commencement of the Constitution?
questions.a: It was the day on which Purna Swaraj Day had been celebrated in 1930, after the Lahore Session resolution of the Congress
o: It was the day on which Purna Swaraj Day had been celebrated in 1930, after the Lahore Session resolution of the Congress

questions.q:

concepts.name: What shaped the Indian Constitution
concepts.description: The influence of the freedom movement, India's civilisational heritage and other countries' constitutions.
concepts.idea: The Constitution draws on the freedom struggle, Indian heritage and ideas from other countries.
concepts.rule: The Constitution had three main influences. The freedom movement gave ideals such as equality, justice, freedom, fraternity and the Constitution as a tool, and many leaders sat in the Assembly. India's civilisational heritage gave ideas such as acceptance of different views, Nature as sacred, respect for women, vasudhaiva kutumbakam and sarve bhavantu sukhinah; Fundamental Duties reflect the emphasis on duties. Following the tradition of 'let noble thoughts come from every side', the makers studied the constitutions of France, USA, UK, Ireland and Australia: liberty, equality, fraternity came from France, Directive Principles from Ireland and an independent judiciary from the USA.
concepts.example: The text was hand-written and illustrated with scenes from Indian history.

concepts.idea: Fundamental Rights can be enforced in court, while Directive Principles are goals for the government.
concepts.rule: The legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary ensures laws follow the Constitution and decides on breaches. India has three tiers: central, state and local (Panchayati Raj). The Constitution defines roles and an electoral system so every eligible citizen can vote. Fundamental Rights, such as equality before law (Article 14), protection of life and liberty (Article 21) and right against exploitation, are promises that can be demanded in court. Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), such as Articles 38, 41, 47, 48-A and 49, are goals that cannot be enforced in court. concepts.name: The Preamble: guiding values of the Constitution
concepts.description: The Preamble and the meaning of sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic, justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
concepts.idea: The Preamble states the values that guide the Constitution.
concepts.rule: The Preamble begins with 'We, the People of India', meaning the Constitution was drawn up by the people through their representatives, not handed down by a king or outside power. Sovereign means the people have the supreme right to decide internal and external matters. Socialist means wealth is generated socially and should be shared, with inequalities reduced. Secular means complete freedom to follow any religion with no official religion. Democratic means the people elect their rulers and hold them accountable. Republic means the head of state is elected. Justice means no discrimination by caste, religion or gender. Liberty means no unreasonable restrictions on thought and expression. Equality means all are equal before law. The terms Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
concepts.example: A person need not take permission from the State to practise rituals of their religion if it harms no one.

questions.q: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 added which three words to the Preamble?
questions.e: The Preamble has been amended by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), which added three new words, Socialist, Secular and Integrity. Class 7 Social Science chapter text (Exploring Society, Grade 7 Part 1, ch.10)notes the same.
w: 'Sovereign' was in the original Preamble.
'Democratic' and 'Unity' were in the original; 'Integrity' was added.
'Fraternity' was in the original Preamble.

questions.q: Which one of the following Supreme Court cases rejected the earlier opinion and held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution?
questions.e: In Berubari (1960) the Court opined that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it rejected that opinion; in the LIC case (1995) it again held the Preamble an integral part. Minerva Mills (1980) is associated with the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, a different point.
w: Berubari held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
LIC (1995) reaffirmed the later position; it did not first reverse Berubari.
Minerva Mills concerns the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles and limits on the amending power, not this point.

questions.q: The term 'republic' in the Preamble indicates that India

The President is elected, not chosen by the Prime Minister.

questions.q: The Indian Constitution embodies which concept of secularism?
questions.a: The positive concept: all religions have equal status and support from the State
o: The positive concept: all religions have equal status and support from the State

The concept of an official religion, with equal tolerance shown to all the other religions
The concept under which the State is anti-religious and condemns all religions equally
questions.e: The Constitution embodies the positive concept of secularism, giving equal respect to all religions. An atheistic state is anti-religious, a theocratic state has an official religion, and a secular state gives equal respect to all; India has no official religion.

The Indian State has no official religion; an official religion with tolerance for others is not the Indian model.
That describes an atheistic state, not a secular one.
